title: Data Quality Investigation (Lab)
summary: Teams run a fair test across four versions of one dataset, record how each output shifts from the clean baseline, and rank the datasets with output evidence.
objectives: Run a hands-on comparison of clean vs noisy data and record how the output changes.
Rank data sets by expected output quality and justify the order.
Use evidence from the comparison, rather than opinion, to explain the data-to-output link.

sections.heading: Data Quality Investigation (Lab)
body: In the Core lesson you predicted one AI mistake from its data. Today you run a proper investigation: four versions of the same dataset, four sets of outputs, and one big question - which data quality problem does the most damage? By the end you will rank them and defend your order with evidence, just like a real AI auditor.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a fair comparison of clean and noisy data and record what changes in the output.
I can rank several datasets from best to worst expected output and justify my ranking.
I can use evidence from the comparison to explain the data-to-output link.

terms.definition: A comparison where you change only one thing so you can tell what caused a result.
The clean result you compare all other versions against.
A specific observation that supports a claim.
Ordering items from best to worst using a clear reason.
A careful check of data or a system before you trust it.

sections.heading: Make the comparison fair
body: To find out how data quality changes an output, you must be fair: keep the task and the model the same, and change only the dataset.
Then any difference you see in the output can be traced back to the data - that is what makes your evidence trustworthy.

sections.heading: Rank with evidence
body: After you see how each dataset changed the output, you rank them from best to worst expected quality.
The hard part is the middle: when two datasets are both weak, you decide which flaw hurt the output more, and you point to the exact output change that proves it.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Your team compares four output sets against a clean baseline, records what changed, and ranks the datasets from best to worst with evidence.
items: Study the clean baseline output so you know what correct looks like.
For each degraded version, write exactly how the output changed.
Match each change to its data flaw.
Score each dataset on accuracy, completeness, and consistency.
Place all four on the ranking line and justify the order.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which data flaw did the most damage, and what evidence proves it?
When two datasets are both weak, how did your team decide which was worse?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one output change that most convinced you of your top ranking.
Describe how you would audit a dataset before trusting an AI built on it.

worksheet.title: Week 1 - Lab - Worksheet | Data Quality Investigation (Lab)

questions.prompt:
A team ran the same task with the same model on four versions of one dataset, and scored each against the clean baseline.

Version A (clean set): 19 of 20 correct.
Version B (blurry photos, labels spelled three ways): 14 of 20 correct, and many answers were unsure.
Version C (no yellow dates in the set): 11 of 20 correct - every yellow date wrong, the rest right.
Version D (some stones labelled "date"): 7 of 20 correct, and it repeated wrong labels confidently.

Rank the four versions by how many of the 20 items each one got right, best first.

items.text: Version B - blurry photos and labels spelled three ways
Version C - no yellow dates in the set

feedback.correct: That is a ranking built on evidence: the order follows what the outputs actually did, from 19 of 20 correct down to 7 of 20 with confident wrong labels.
feedback.incorrect: Rank by what each version's output did, not by how bad the flaw sounds - match each version back to its recorded score before placing it on the line.

questions.prompt: The team wants their investigation to show that the differences in the outputs really came from the data. Which plan makes it a fair test?

options.text: Keep the task and the model the same for every version, and change only the dataset.
Give each dataset a different model, so every dataset gets its best chance.
Change the dataset and make the task harder at the same time, so the differences are easier to see.
Test each dataset on a different task, then compare the average scores.

feedback.correct: Exactly - when only the dataset changes, any difference in the output can be traced back to the data, and that is what makes your evidence trustworthy.
feedback.incorrect: If more than one thing changes between versions, you can no longer tell whether the data or the other change caused the difference.

questions.prompt: A ranking has to be justified with evidence from the outputs, not opinion. Select every line below that counts as evidence.

options.text: The error version called 3 of the 5 stones "date"; the clean version called none of them dates.
The noisy version got 14 of 20 right - six fewer than the clean baseline.
The gap version got every yellow date wrong, while the baseline got all of them right.
Our team all agreed that the noisy dataset felt like the worst one.
The error version must be worst, because wrong data is always the worst thing.

feedback.correct: Yes - evidence is a specific observation of what the output did, and each of those points to an exact change you could show someone.
feedback.incorrect: Agreeing as a team or stating a general rule is not evidence; evidence names the exact output change, such as how many items shifted from right to wrong.

questions.prompt: Match each change the team saw in the output to the data flaw responsible for it.

left.text: It gives a wrong name to certain items, and repeats the same wrong name confidently every time.
It gets every example of one whole category wrong, but handles the other categories well.
Its answers are unsure and inconsistent across every kind of item, with no one category failing more than the rest.
Its answers stay close to the baseline on every kind of item.

right.text: Wrong labels in the training data (an error)
A missing category in the training data (a gap)
Blurry photos and labels spelled three different ways (noise)
No flaw - this is the clean dataset

feedback.correct: Well matched - each flaw leaves its own fingerprint: an error is confident and repeated, a gap hits one category only, and noise spreads uncertainty everywhere.
feedback.incorrect: Look at where the damage lands: one category only points to a gap, confident repeated wrong names point to wrong labels, and uncertainty across everything points to noise.

questions.prompt: Complete this line from the team's investigation log: "We kept the task and the model the same and changed only the (1), and we compared every version against the clean result, which we call the (2)."
blanks: (1) the one thing they changed between versions
(2) the name for the clean result everything is compared against

feedback.correct: That is the whole method in one line: change only the dataset, and measure every version against the baseline so your evidence means something.
feedback.incorrect: Only one thing changes in a fair test - the dataset - and the clean result you compare everything against is the baseline.

formative.targets: Grade 5 Advanced: explains how data quality affects AI outputs
formative.check: Four-way contrast plus ranking task with written justification
formative.successCriteria: Ranks datasets by expected output quality and justifies the order using evidence from the output changes.
formative.evidence: Investigation log and ranking line with justification.
